labels.text: Asks before file edits and commands that need approval.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Mode and reasoning effort" button > Mode > Auto
steps: Open AGI Code and click the "Mode and reasoning effort" button.
Pick Mode > Auto.
Send a request that reads files and makes an ordinary edit.
Look: ordinary edits and safe commands run without a card, while other commands show an "Approval needed" card.
items.needs: An AGI account signed in.
items.note: Auto covers edits and safe commands. It does not split reads from risky actions as Expected describes.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card (summary line and risk words)
steps: Trigger an approval in Ask mode (see S59.01).
Read the card title "Approval needed" and the summary line under it.
Read the risk word, such as "Low risk", "Medium risk" or "High risk", and whether it says "Can be undone" or "Cannot be undone".
Look: the summary says what the tool will do; check whether it also says why approval is needed.
items.needs: An AGI account signed in, and a request that triggers a tool approval.
items.note: The card shows the summary and risk only. An explicit "why" line was not found.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card for a send action > "Sends to:" row
steps: Ask AGI to send a message in a tool that has a recipient, such as an email or chat connector, in Ask mode.
Wait for the "Approval needed" card.
Look for the row "Sends to:" and check it names the exact recipients.
items.needs: A send-type connector tool and a request that uses it.
items.note: The row shows only when the tool arguments contain a recipient field (to, cc, channel and similar).

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card (summary and detail text)
steps: Trigger an outbound action in Ask mode, such as a fetch to a web address.
Wait for the "Approval needed" card.
Look for the exact URL or host in the summary or the detail block.
Check it matches the destination the agent will use.
items.needs: A request that makes an outbound call.
items.note: The card has no separate destination row. The host or URL appears only if the summary or detail text includes it.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card for a purchase > "Amount:" and "For:" rows
steps: Ask AGI to make a purchase or payment through a connector, in Ask mode.
Wait for the "Approval needed" card.
Look for the "Amount:" row with the value and currency, and the "For:" row with the item.
Check they match what the purchase will buy.
items.needs: A purchase-type connector tool and a request that uses it.
items.note: The rows appear only when the tool arguments contain amount and item fields.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card for a command > detail box under the summary
steps: Ask AGI to run a shell command in Ask mode, such as npm test.
Wait for the "Approval needed" card.
Read the detail box under the summary.
Look: it shows the exact command line. Check whether it also shows where it runs.
items.needs: A request that runs a shell command.
items.note: No separate working-folder line was found on the card.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card for a file write > summary and detail, plus "Review change"
steps: Ask AGI to edit a file in Ask mode.
Wait for the "Approval needed" card.
Read the summary and the detail box for the files named.
Look: check the exact files that will change match the request.
items.needs: A request that edits files.
items.note: No separate file-list row was found. The file names come only from the summary or detail text.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card for a file edit > "Review change" button
steps: Ask AGI to edit a file in Ask mode.
On the "Approval needed" card, click "Review change".
Look: the proposed file opens in a VS Code diff editor.
Edit or revert part of it, then approve, and check the file is written with your version.
items.needs: A file-edit request that produces a proposed change.
items.note: The button shows only when the request has a proposed change (reviewable).

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card > "Approve once"
steps: Trigger an approval in Ask mode.
Click "Approve once" on the card.
Look: the card shows the outcome as allowed, and the action runs and its result appears in the transcript.
items.needs: An AGI account signed in, and a request that triggers a tool approval.
items.note: The visible word is "Approve once", not "Allow".

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card > "Deny"
steps: Trigger an approval in Ask mode.
Click "Deny" on the card.
Look: the card shows "Denied.", the action does not run, and the transcript continues.
Check the agent's next message reflects the refusal.
items.needs: An AGI account signed in, and a request that triggers a tool approval.
items.note: That the model is told about the denial was not checked from the UI.

items.where: AGI Code panel > "Approval needed" card > text box at the bottom
steps: Trigger an approval in Ask mode.
Click the text box at the bottom of the card, labelled "Or deny and tell AGI what to do instead, then press Enter".
Type guidance, for example "use a different file", and press Enter.
Look: the card shows Denied, and the agent continues with your guidance in the next message.
items.needs: An AGI account signed in, and a request that triggers a tool approval.

labels.text: Or deny and tell AGI what to do instead, then press Enter

items.where: On the "Approval needed" card in the AGI Code panel
steps: Trigger an approval in Ask mode and leave the card unanswered.
Wait about 10 minutes.
Look: the card should show that the turn ended before it was answered, and the action should not run.
items.needs: A card left unanswered for the full wait.

labels.text: The turn ended before this was answered.

items.note: The 10-minute timer is set in apps/cli/src/app_server/developer_host.rs (APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 600). Whether a timeout reaches this card as the expired text was not confirmed.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Show Approval History"
steps: Sign in with "Code: Sign In to AGI Cloud".
Run "Code: Show Approval History" from the Command Palette.
Look: a list titled "Code, Approval history" shows past approvals with "Approved" or "Denied" and a time.
Pick a row with a conversation to open it in the browser.
items.needs: Signed in to AGI Cloud, with some past approvals.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" > task row with the check icon (tooltip "Approve this run")
steps: On device A, start a cloud task that waits for approval.
On device B, signed in to the same account, run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" and pick the waiting task.
Click the row icon with tooltip "Approve this run" or "Reject this run".
On device A, run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" again and look: the task shows its new state.
If device B already answered, the message reads that another device already answered this one.
items.needs: Two devices signed in to AGI Cloud on the same account, and a cloud task waiting for approval.
items.note: The first device is shown the result on its next refresh of the list, not live.

items.where: VS Code notification when an approval is needed (buttons "Allow once", "Deny", "Open chat")
steps: Set Mode to Ask in AGI Code.
Switch to another app so the VS Code window is not focused.
Send a request that needs approval.
Look for the VS Code notification "Code: ..." with the summary and the buttons "Allow once" and "Deny". Click "Allow once" and check the action runs.
items.needs: Two apps open (VS Code and another), and an AGI account signed in.
items.note: The alert fires only when the VS Code window is not focused. It is a VS Code message, not a macOS notification; questions show only "Open chat".

items.where: Chat panel > a request that makes the agent do something irreversible (for example delete a file or send a message) > the approval card shows "Cannot be undone" and has no "Approve for session" button
steps: Sign in, open a workspace folder, and open the AGI chat panel.
Send a request that asks the agent to delete a file or send a message, which cannot be undone.
When the approval card appears, look for the line "Cannot be undone" on the card.
Check the card's buttons: "Approve once" and "Deny" should be there, and "Approve for session" should be missing.
Compare with Expected: the warning is shown and no permanent allow is offered.
items.needs: a signed-in account and a workspace folder open in VS Code
items.note: Which actions lose the session button depends on the action kind and the host's requiresExplicitDecision flag; a second stronger warning, "Turn on Bypass Permissions?" (modal), appears at Mode and reasoning effort > Bypass permissions.

items.where: Chat panel > a request that needs approval > click "Approve once" on the approval card > the same reply continues
steps: Sign in, open a workspace folder, and open the AGI chat panel.
Send a request that makes the agent run a command or edit a file, so an approval card appears.
Click the "Approve once" button on the approval card.
Watch the same reply: the tool runs and the agent carries on in that turn without you sending a new message.
Compare with Expected: the same run resumes where it stopped.
items.needs: a signed-in account and a workspace folder open in VS Code
items.note: The resume is driven by the 'turnResumed' message in the webview; the exact tool that triggers an approval depends on the mode chosen.

items.where: Chat panel > approval card > click "Approve once" or "Deny" or "Abort turn" > the card shows the decision ("Allowed once.", "Denied.", or "Turn aborted.") and the tool result follows
steps: Sign in, open a workspace folder, and open the AGI chat panel.
Send a request that makes the agent edit a file, so an approval card appears with a diff.
Click "Approve once" and look at the card: it should show "Allowed once." under the decision.
Look at the tool entry below it for the result of the action, or for "Open diff" for a file edit.
Repeat with "Deny" and check the card shows "Denied." and the tool does not run.
Compare with Expected: the transcript shows what was decided and what happened.
items.needs: a signed-in account and a workspace folder open in VS Code
items.note: The outcome lines are built from constants ("Allowed" + " once.", "Denied" + "."), so the full sentences are not written out in one file.

items.where: Message box > "/" (Commands) > /cloud, or Command Palette > Code: Continue in the Cloud
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud, and open a folder whose git branch is pushed to GitHub.
Click the "/" button (title "Commands") under the message box and choose /cloud. Or open the Command Palette and run "Code: Continue in the Cloud".
In the input box titled "Continue in the cloud", type what the task should do and press Enter.
In the review dialog, check the repository, branch and model, then click "Continue in the cloud".
Watch for the progress notification "starting a cloud session", then the result message. Compare with Expected: a cloud agent run has started and can be found under Work > Cloud tasks.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account and a checked-out branch that is pushed to GitHub
items.note: This is a cloud session on a branch, not a separate work-task screen. The entry is the only one found that describes and starts a cloud agent run.

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > pick a task > Rename task
steps: Click the "More" button in the sidebar header (aria label "More actions") and choose Work.
Under Cloud tasks, pick a task row that has a conversation.
Choose "Rename task", type a new name and press Enter.
Compare with Expected: the list row and the detail title show the new name. The row title is otherwise the first line of the task's conversation title, or a default such as "AGI work task".
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account and a cloud task that has a conversation
items.note: Rename is offered only when the task has a conversation.

items.where: Message box > "/" (Commands) > /cloud, then type the objective in the "Continue in the cloud" box
steps: Start the flow as in S60.01: choose /cloud or run "Code: Continue in the Cloud".
In the input box titled "Continue in the cloud", type the objective. The prompt names the branch.
Click "Continue in the cloud" in the review dialog.
Open More actions > Work > Cloud tasks and find the new task. Compare with Expected: the objective is stored with the run and shown back.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account and a pushed branch
items.note: Code shows the objective is sent as the agent turn and its first line becomes the task title. Whether the full objective is shown back in the task view was not confirmed in the code.

items.where: Message box > "+" (Attach or use tools) > Add context
steps: Click the "+" button (title "Attach or use tools") under the message box.
Read the "Add context" menu: "Attach workspace files", "Selection", "Open editors", "Problems", "Git changes", "Terminal output", "Web page".
Choose one, for example "Git changes".
Compare with Expected: the chosen source appears as an item above the message box before you send.
items.needs: none for the menu; an open project folder for workspace files
items.note: A cloud continuation has no source picker: the repository and branch are fixed in the review dialog. Connectors are a separate surface (More actions > Connectors), not in this menu.

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Choose Tools for This Session
steps: Open the Command Palette and run "Code: Choose Tools for This Session".
Tick or untick the tools: "Shell commands", "File edits", "New files", "Web search", "Web pages", "Browser".
Press Enter to confirm.
Send a message and compare with Expected: the unticked tools are not used. The picker says the choice applies from your next message.
items.needs: a local runtime that supports tool filters; otherwise an error message appears

labels.text: Code: Choose Tools for This Session

items.note: This picker is for the local session, not for cloud tasks.

items.where: Message box > model pill (shows "Auto") > pick a model in "Select model"
steps: Find the pill under the message box, showing "Auto" by default (title "Model").
Click it. The popover "Select model" opens.
Choose a model from the list.
Compare with Expected: the pill shows the chosen model before you send. Command Palette "Code: Select Model" offers the same choice.
items.needs: none
items.note: The code shows the model is sent with the turn, but whether the run records it was not confirmed. A cloud continuation takes its model from the configured setting and shows it in the review dialog.

items.where: Message box > "Mode and reasoning effort" button > Effort, or Command Palette > Code: Set Reasoning Effort
steps: Click the "Mode and reasoning effort" button under the message box, or run "Code: Set Reasoning Effort" from the Command Palette.
Pick an effort level: None, Minimal, Low, Medium, High, xHigh or Max.
Compare with Expected: a message "AGI Code effort set to: <level>" appears (palette route), and the controls show the new level.
Send a message. The effort is sent with the turn in the local chat code path.
items.needs: none
items.note: A cloud continuation sends only the goal and model in the code read, so the effort setting is not sent with a cloud task.

items.where: Message box > "+" (Attach or use tools) > Plan mode, then send a task
steps: Click "+" (title "Attach or use tools") and choose "Plan mode".
Send a task such as a small refactor.
Wait until the card titled "Plan" stops streaming.

Compare with Expected: the buttons "Approve and auto-accept edits" and "Revise" appear. Click "Revise" to see the box "What should change in the plan?" with "Send" and "Cancel". Nothing runs until you approve.
items.needs: none
items.note: The approve button's words say it also auto-accepts edits. Editing is done through Revise; there is no direct step editor in the code read.

items.where: Message box > card titled "Plan" (after Plan mode); for cloud runs: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > pick a task > Progress
steps: In Plan mode, send a task and open the card titled "Plan" in the chat.
Read the count (for example "2/5 complete") and the list of steps.
For a cloud run, click "More" (More actions) > Work > Cloud tasks > pick a task.
Compare with Expected: the "Progress" section lists each step with its own status icon, matching the run.
items.needs: a Plan-mode turn for the chat card, or a cloud task for the Progress list

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > Working > pick a running task > Progress
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work, then open the group "Working" under Cloud tasks.
Pick a running task.
In the "Progress" section, find the step with a spinning icon. That is the step executing now.
Compare with Expected: the spinner moves to the next step as the run continues.
items.needs: a cloud task that is running
items.note: The running marker is an icon (spinner) with no text, so the tester must look at it.

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > Needs you > pick a task > Actions > Approve
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work and open the group "Needs you" under Cloud tasks.
Pick a task. In its detail, under "Actions", read the tool names shown next to "Approve" and "Reject".
Click "Approve". A modal dialog asks to approve. Confirm with "Approve and continue".
Compare with Expected: the task leaves "Needs you" and continues. Choosing "Reject" asks for an optional reason.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account and a cloud task waiting for a tool approval

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > pick a working task > Message the agent
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work and pick a task in the group "Working".
In its detail, click "Message the agent" (description "Add instructions or change course").
Type the guidance in the box and press Enter. The prompt says it reads the message at its next step.
Compare with Expected: a notification "Queued. The agent reads it at its next step." appears. Reopen the task and see "Your messages" with the message marked as queued.
items.needs: a cloud task in the state queued, planning, running or resuming
a paused or stopped cloud task
items.note: Searched features/cloud-tasks (cloudRunDetail.ts, cloudRunApproval.ts, cloudTasksTree.ts) for resume. The only resumeRun call is inside approve or reject. No Resume control was found, and paused tasks are not steerable.

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > pick a running task > Stop this task
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work and pick a task that is still running.
Click "Stop this task" (description "Asks the cloud executor to cancel the run").
In the modal dialog that asks Stop "<task title>"?, click "Stop this task" to confirm.
Compare with Expected: the notification "This task was asked to stop." appears, and the task moves to "Stopped".
items.needs: a cloud task that is still running
items.note: The item is not shown for a task that has already settled.

items.needs: a finished cloud task
items.note: Searched features/cloud-tasks, features/surfaces, core/commandSetup.ts and features/chat/retry.ts for restart. The only match is "Code: Retry Last Message", which resends the last chat message. No restart control for a finished cloud task was found.

items.needs: none
items.note: Searched features/cloud-tasks, features/surfaces and core/commandSetup.ts for duplicate. None for cloud tasks. The closest is "Code: Fork Conversation", which forks a local session, not a cloud task.

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > Done > pick a task > Result
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work and open the group "Done" under Cloud tasks.
Pick a finished task.
Read the "Result" section, which shows the first line of the result, with the detail "Select to copy the full result".
Compare with Expected: the result summary matches what the run produced. Selecting the line copies the full result with the notice "copied the task result".
items.needs: a finished cloud task (completed, ready for review or archived)

labels.text: Select to copy the full result

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > pick a task > Outputs
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work and pick a task that produced files.
Read the "Outputs" section, which lists each file by its title (or "Untitled" plus its type).
Select a file.
Compare with Expected: the file opens in the editor. The code opens the file; it has no download step.
items.needs: a cloud task linked to a conversation that produced an artifact
items.note: Outputs appear only for tasks that have a conversation. Code opens the file; it has no download action.

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks > Stopped > pick a task > Outcome
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work and open the group "Stopped" under Cloud tasks.
Pick a task that stopped short.
Read the "Outcome" section, for example "2 of 5 steps done, 3 not finished".
Compare with Expected: the done and remaining steps match the Progress list.
items.needs: a cloud task that ended as partial, failed, cancelled or timed out, with steps

items.where: More actions > Work, or Command Palette > Code: Show Cloud Tasks
steps: Click "More" (More actions) > Work, or run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" from the Command Palette.
Look at the groups "Needs you", "Working", "Ready for review", "Done" and "Stopped", each with its tasks.
Read each row's title and state.
Pick any row to open its detail. Compare with Expected: the list refreshes about every 15 seconds and can be refreshed with the refresh button.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account that has cloud tasks
items.note: The list shows at most one page of 25 runs per load (CLOUD_TASKS_PAGE_LIMIT).

items.where: More actions > Work > Cloud tasks (tasks from other devices appear here), then pick a task
steps: On a second device (web, desktop or another VS Code), start a task with the same AGI Cloud account.
In VS Code, open More actions > Work and find the task under Cloud tasks. Use the refresh button if it has not appeared.
Open the task, then use "Message the agent", "Approve" or "Stop this task".
Compare with Expected: the change is applied and the state shown on the other device follows it. Use "Open on web" to open the conversation in a browser.
items.needs: a second device or the web, signed into the same AGI Cloud account
items.note: Cross-device following relies on the account and the list refresh, which the code read could not confirm end to end.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" (quick pick ending in "Cloud tasks"; the runs sit under group headings such as "Working")
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud (the list needs an AGI account; if signed out, the list shows "Sign in to see your cloud tasks").
Start two or more cloud tasks, or use an account that already has them running.
Open the Command Palette and run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks".
Look at the list: several runs should appear at the same time, grouped under "Working" (and other groups), each with its own row.
Click "Refresh cloud tasks" in the title bar of the list and check that the states update.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI account with two or more cloud tasks running
items.note: The list is a quick pick, not a live pane: no automatic refresh is wired in src (setAutoRefreshEnabled is only called from tests), so the tester must use Refresh to see changes. The cited line numbers in the plan were out of date; the grouping code is at cloudTasksTree.ts lines 45-52.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Show Cloud Tasks", then the first group "Needs you"
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud and have at least one cloud task that is waiting for your input or for approval, and at least one task that is running.
Open the Command Palette and run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks".
Look at the group order: "Needs you" should be the first group, above "Working", "Ready for review", "Done" and "Stopped".
Compare: the waiting task should be listed under "Needs you" and not under "Working".
items.needs: a signed-in AGI account with a cloud task waiting for input or approval, and one running task
items.note: The ordering is fixed in STAGE_GROUPS (cloudTasksTree.ts lines 45-52); the plan's cited lines 27 and 110 no longer hold the quoted code. Only the group order is shown; rows inside a group follow the server's page order.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Show Cloud Tasks", then a row under "Needs you" with the check and x row buttons
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud and have a cloud task with a pending approval (it shows under "Needs you").
Open the Command Palette and run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" and stay in the list.
Hover the check button on the waiting row: the tooltip should read "Approve this run". Hover the x button: "Reject this run".
Click the check button, read the confirmation (it offers "Approve and continue"), and confirm.
Compare: the list should update and the run should leave "Needs you"; the x button rejects the run and asks for a reason.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI account with a cloud task that has a pending approval
items.note: The row buttons appear only on runs with a pending approval (contextValue cloudRunPendingApproval). The same approve and reject choices are also in the run's detail pick ("Approve" and "Reject", cloudRunDetail.ts). Input requests, unlike approvals, have no inline button in the code.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Continue in the Cloud" (hands the current branch to a cloud session; the cloud session then continues the work and shows under "Code: Show Cloud Tasks")
steps: Open a folder whose git remote is on GitHub, check out a branch, and push it (the code refuses a detached commit or an unpushed branch).
Open the Command Palette and run "Code: Continue in the Cloud".
Read the review message, choose the continue option, and confirm the repository, branch and model shown.
Open the Command Palette and run "Code: Show Cloud Tasks" to find the new cloud task.
Open the new task (or "Code: Open AGI Code Session") and check that the cloud session continues the work from that branch.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account, a workspace with a GitHub remote, and a pushed branch
items.note: The code's handoff is local-to-cloud ("Continue in the cloud"), not agent-to-agent; the plan's cited file cloudCodeSessions.ts line 184 shows a session transcript row, not a handoff control. There is also a "Continue in the cloud" icon button in the chat's Sessions sheet, shown only on the Cloud tab. The exact confirmation wording comes from translation keys (cloud.continueQuestion) that were not checked.

items.where: Chat: "/" button (title "Commands") > Context > "Rewind" > pick a prompt under "Checkpoints" > "Fork conversation and rewind code"; or Command Palette > "Code: Fork Conversation"
steps: Open the AGI chat in the editor and send a prompt that changes a file, so a checkpoint exists.
Click the "/" button titled "Commands", then choose "Rewind" under Context.
In the list titled "Checkpoints", pick the prompt to go back to.
Choose "Fork conversation and rewind code" and confirm.
Compare: a new chat should open just before that prompt, the original chat keeps its history, and you can keep typing in the new chat.
items.needs: a developer session with a prompt that changed tracked files; the fork option appears only when the runtime offers it
items.note: The fork option is offered only when the checkpoint has both a conversation point and tracked files, and when the runtime offers forkAndRewind. The Command Palette "Code: Fork Conversation" route forks a whole session (asks for a name, default "<title> (fork)") and is not tied to a point in the conversation; it has no menu entry in package.json.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules row, click the play icon tooltipped "Run now" (also in the Command Palette as "Code: Run Schedule Now")
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work. In the Schedules part, hover an active schedule and click the play icon "Run now".
In the modal, click "Run it now".
Read the message that appears. Then click "Show recent runs" on the same schedule and check the newest run.
Compare with Expected: the run starts straight away and the run history shows it completing with a result.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with an active, enabled schedule
items.note: The message after the click only reports that the run started; the finished result appears later in run history. The Run now icon also shows on paused schedules, where the click is refused with a message saying the schedule must be active and enabled.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules (each row's description line)
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work.
Read the description line on each schedule row.
Look for the next-run part: a future time reads "next in" followed by a duration, a past one reads "due" with "ago", and a paused or completed schedule reads "no next run".
Compare with Expected: each routine shows when it will next run.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with at least one schedule
items.note: The next-run text is shown in the Work list rows, not in a separate tree view; the Command Palette command "Code: Show Schedules" opens the same list.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules (each row's description line)
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work.
Read the description line on each schedule row for the last-run part.
Look for "last ran" followed by a time, "never run", or "last run failed".
Compare with Expected: each routine shows when it last ran and whether that run failed.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with a schedule that has run at least once, and ideally one whose last run failed
items.note: "last run failed" appears only when the schedule carries a last error; the failure text itself is in the hover tooltip.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules row, click the history icon "Show recent runs" (also "Code: Show Schedule Runs" in the Command Palette)
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work.
Hover a schedule row and click the history icon "Show recent runs".
If the schedule has never run, read the message saying it has not run yet. Otherwise read the list titled "Runs of" followed by the schedule name.
Compare with Expected: each past run shows its status and time, such as "Succeeded · <time>", newest first.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with a schedule that has past runs
items.note: The list shows the newest 20 runs only.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules row, click "Show recent runs", then pick a run in the list
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work, then hover a schedule row and click "Show recent runs".
Pick a run that has an answer. The list placeholder reads "Pick a run to read its answer".
Read the text tab that opens. It has the schedule name as a heading, the run status line, and then the run's output text.
Compare with Expected: the run's output text is shown, not only its status. A run with no output opens nothing.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with a schedule that has a run with output

labels.text: Pick a run to read its answer

items.note: The extension keeps a run's answer in memory for the session; if it is no longer held, the tab says "This run's answer is no longer held here."

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules row, click the icon "Pause this schedule" or "Resume this schedule" (also "Code: Pause Schedule" and "Code: Resume Schedule" in the Command Palette)
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work. Hover an active schedule and click "Pause this schedule".
Read the progress message "pausing" and then check that the row description says "Paused".
Hover the same row and click "Resume this schedule".
Compare with Expected: the schedule pauses and resumes, and it stays in the list the whole time (nothing is deleted).
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with an active schedule
items.note: A schedule that cannot be paused or resumed in its current state shows the message "this schedule cannot be paused or resumed in its current state." instead.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules row, click "Show recent runs", then pick the run labelled "Waiting for approval"
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar and use a schedule whose run is waiting for approval (set up on the web).
Click More, then Work. Read the row description: it includes "a run is waiting for your approval".
Hover the schedule and click "Show recent runs". Pick the run whose status is "Waiting for approval".

items.where: AGI Code sidebar > More > Work > Schedules row, click "Show recent runs"
steps: Sign in to AGI Cloud from the AGI Code sidebar.
Click More, then Work. Hover a schedule that has a missed or skipped run and click "Show recent runs".
Find the run whose label starts with "Skipped" (or "Ran late" in its detail).

Read the detail text after the first dot separators. A missed run reads like "Skipped the run scheduled for <time>: it was missed by <duration>, and this schedule skips missed runs." A late run reads "Ran late: scheduled for <time>, started <duration> later."
Compare with Expected: the run history says that the occurrence was missed or skipped, and why.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI Cloud account with a schedule that has missed or skipped a run (not something the app can create on demand)
items.note: The explanation shows only when the run record holds missed-run details, which the extension reads and does not create; the reason appears in the run's detail text, not on the schedule row.

Click OK in the box. The page is read once from that link and its text is attached to the next message.
Type a question about the page and send it. Compare: the answer uses the text of the pasted link, not the page open in your browser tab.

items.note: VS Code only reads a pasted link, not the live browser page; the live-page reading in the Chrome side panel (apps/extension) was not traced to a label. The plus button's own label was not confirmed.

Type a question after it and send. Compare: the answer uses the highlighted text as context.

items.note: The exact button label in the Chrome dialog that starts the send was not found in the code; the destination name "VS Code" was found.

items.where: Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) > "Code: Permissions" (or type "/permissions" in the chat box) > "Trusted folders" section > trash icon on a folder > "Stop Trusting"
steps: Open the AGI chat panel in VS Code, then press Cmd+Shift+P and type "Code: Permissions". Press Enter. (Or type /permissions in the chat box.)
Look for the separator "Trusted folders" in the list. Each trusted folder shows its path, with the description "The agent may read, edit and run commands here".
Hover a folder row and click its trash icon (tooltip "Stop trusting").

In the dialog, click "Stop Trusting". Then reopen Code: Permissions and check that the folder is gone from "Trusted folders". Also check that the folder now reads "No folders are trusted yet" if it was the only one.
To grant a folder, open it in VS Code and accept VS Code's own Workspace Trust prompt (not AGI's). Then check that "Trusted folders" lists it under Code: Permissions.
items.needs: A paid or Free account that can sign in, a folder that is trusted in VS Code, and an AGI CLI that offers trusted folders (the "Trusted folders" section only appears when the CLI reports it)
items.note: Revoke is in the UI, but granting is not: AGI has no add-folder control in the Permissions view. A folder gets its grant from VS Code Workspace Trust (extension.ts:353 records consent on trust grant), and the 'Restricted Mode' message in localRuntimeClient.ts:118 tells the person to trust the folder. The VS Code trust prompt itself is outside this app's code. The Permissions view appears only when the CLI offers permission rules; the trusted-folder rows appear only when it offers trust. Both conditions are unverified at runtime.

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Open Chat", then the box "Describe a task…"
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Open Chat" and press Enter.
Click the box that says "Describe a task…" and type a migration request, for example: Replace every use of the old function name with the new one across the repository.
Press Enter and wait for the agent to finish.
Compare with Expected: the changes should appear across several files, shown as proposals with Accept and Reject.
items.needs: a trusted workspace folder open, with the developer runtime set up

items.where: Command Palette > "Code: Open Chat", then the box "Describe a task…"
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Open Chat" and press Enter.
Click the box that says "Describe a task…" and type: Upgrade the dependency named in package.json to its newest version and adjust the code to it.
Press Enter and wait for the agent to finish.
Compare with Expected: the manifest and the affected code should change, shown as proposals with Accept and Reject.
items.needs: a trusted workspace folder open, with the developer runtime set up

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Git Commit
steps: Open a folder that is a git repository with changes, in VS Code.
Press Cmd+Shift+P and type "Code: Git Commit", then press Enter.
In the box labelled "Commit message", type a message such as "feat: test commit", then press Enter.
Open the Source Control view and the git history, and look for a new commit with that message and the changes in it.
items.needs: a git repository open in VS Code with uncommitted changes
items.note: The command is listed only in the Command Palette. I did not check whether the agent in chat can commit on its own, so that part of Expected is unverified from the code.

items.where: Command Palette > Code: New Session in a Worktree (or Code: Session Worktrees, then a name)
steps: Open a git repository folder in VS Code.
Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: New Session in a Worktree", then press Enter.
Or press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Session Worktrees", choose the named option, and type a name in the box labelled "Enter a worktree name".
A new window opens on the new worktree folder. Check that the branch name shown for it in the list is not the branch you started from.
items.needs: a git repository open in VS Code

labels.text: Code: New Session in a Worktree

items.note: VS Code has no plain create-branch control. A branch is made through a session worktree, which the CLI creates (apps/cli/src/platform/runtime/git_tools.rs:168 is in the CLI, not this app, and I did not read it). The worktree list shows its branch, and removing a worktree deletes its branch. Branch creation by the agent itself was not checked.

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Create Pull Request
steps: Work on a branch that has commits not yet in the base branch, in a git repository folder.
Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Create Pull Request", then press Enter.
If a warning appears, it names the reason no pull request can be opened. Otherwise, type a title in the box labelled "Pull request title", then answer the next box for the base branch.

If the branch is not pushed yet, click "Push and Open". If it is already pushed, click "Open Pull Request". Look for the message "Code: pull request opened." with a View button, and check the pull request on the code host.
items.needs: a branch with commits and an account on the code host (the exact account requirement was not checked)
items.note: The base-branch prompt text was not read, so the tester should answer it by what it asks. The agent in chat creating a pull request was not checked.

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Remember for This Repository
steps: Open a trusted workspace folder that is a repository.
Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Remember for This Repository", then press Enter.
Choose the repository folder if asked, type a note such as "Run pnpm test:unit before committing" in the box titled "Remember for this repository", then press Enter.
Read the confirmation message. Then start a new session in the same repository and ask the agent what it was told to remember. Compare its answer with the note you saved.
items.needs: a trusted workspace folder that is a repository
items.note: The reuse in later sessions is inner behaviour; the tester sees it only by asking in a new session. The confirmation message's buttons were not fully read, so "Open memory file" is the constant in the file, not confirmed as a visible button.

items.where: More actions (the "..." button at the top of the sidebar) > Instructions
steps: Open a workspace folder that holds AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, and open the AGI sidebar.
Click the "More" (...) button at the top of the sidebar, then click "Instructions".
In the list, pick a file to open it and check it is the repository's instruction file.
Ask the agent a question that one of those rules governs, and check that its answer follows the rule in the file.
items.needs: a workspace folder with AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md
items.note: The Instructions list shows only files the CLI loads, and says "The CLI loads no instruction files in this workspace." when there are none. That the agent follows them is inner behaviour seen only in its answers.

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Show Skills (or More actions > Skills, or type /skills in the chat box)
steps: Open a workspace folder and the AGI sidebar.
Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Show Skills", then press Enter. Or click "More" (...) > "Skills".
If the item "Allow this folder’s project skills" appears, choose it to allow the folder's project skills.
Select a skill, then use its "Turn off" or "Turn on" button (the tooltip on its icon). Ask the agent something a skill covers and compare its answer with the skill's state.
items.needs: a workspace folder with project skills; a second check needs a chat question
items.note: Turn on and Turn off are icon tooltips, not visible words. Plugins are a separate screen (Code: Show Plugins) and were not walked through.

items.where: No control of its own. Its effect shows as the same session title and row in the Sessions sheet on each client
steps: Click the Sessions icon in the sidebar header and note the session title on the Local tab.
Open the same session on the second client and compare the title and row shown with Expected.
items.needs: a second client signed in to the same account
items.note: The Code line cites ChatStateManager.ts:340, which now holds the sendMessage type, not the identifier logic; the session identifier itself has no visible text.

items.where: Sessions icon in the sidebar header > Local tab > click a session row
steps: Click the Sessions icon (tooltip Sessions) in the sidebar header.
Make sure the Local tab is selected, then click a session row.
Compare the conversation history shown with the history on the second client, as Expected.
items.needs: a second client (VS Code, CLI or desktop) signed in to the same account and the same workspace

items.where: Sessions icon in the sidebar header > Cloud tab > look at the branch line under a session row
steps: Click the Sessions icon in the sidebar header.
Click the Cloud tab.
Read the branch text under a session row (shown only when the session has a working branch).
Compare the branch with the branch the same session shows on the second client.
items.needs: a cloud session that has a working branch, and a second client on the same account
items.note: The branch appears as small text on the row with no label of its own.

items.where: Command palette > Code: Continue in the Cloud > type a goal > review dialog line Repository:
steps: Open a folder whose git remote is on GitHub, with its branch pushed.
Open the Command Palette and run Code: Continue in the Cloud.
Type a goal and press Enter.
Read the Repository: line in the review dialog and compare it with the repository on the other client, then click Cancel.
items.needs: a folder with a GitHub git remote and a pushed branch
items.note: The Cloud tab list is filtered to sessions of the repository open in the window, but no row shows the repository name directly.

items.where: Command palette > Code: Session Worktrees
steps: Open the Command Palette and run Code: Session Worktrees.
Read the list of worktrees and the branch named for each one.
Compare the worktree a session is tied to with the worktree shown on the second client.
items.needs: a git repository with at least one session worktree

labels.text: Code: New Session in a Worktree

items.note: The Code line cited sessionWorktrees.ts lines that moved; the command and its worktree list are present in the file.

items.where: No control of its own. Its visible effect is the Model: line in the Code: Continue in the Cloud review dialog
steps: Run Code: Continue in the Cloud, type a goal and press Enter.
Read the Model: line in the review dialog and compare it with the model shown on the second client.
Click Cancel.
items.needs: a folder with a GitHub git remote and a pushed branch
items.note: No screen was found that shows the instruction files a session uses.

items.where: Command palette > Code: Checkpoints
steps: Open a chat with some turns in it.
Open the Command Palette and run Code: Checkpoints.
Read the checkpoints listed for the session, and the Checkpoints item in the chat menu if it shows.
Compare the checkpoints with those on the second client.
items.needs: a session that already has at least one prompt
items.note: No separate task-plan screen was found; the plan appears only in the chat. The Code line cited lines that moved.

items.where: Sessions icon in the sidebar header > Cloud tab > click a session row > Approval required
steps: Click the Sessions icon in the sidebar header and click the Cloud tab.
Click a cloud session that is waiting for an approval.
Read the Approval required section at the top of the list (items show Approve and continue or Reject).
Answer it here, then check the second client shows the answer.
items.needs: a cloud session with a pending approval, and a second client on the same account
items.note: The approve item text is built from Approve plus ' and continue'.

items.where: No control of its own. Its visible effect is tool lines appearing live in an open cloud session while a turn runs
steps: Start a turn in a cloud session from one client.
Open the same session on the second client and watch the progress notice that reads Working while the turn runs.
items.needs: a cloud session that is running a turn, and a second client on the same account
items.note: No separate view of tool activity was found in this app.

items.where: Sessions icon in the sidebar header > Cloud tab > click a session row > Continue here
steps: Click the Sessions icon in the sidebar header and click the Cloud tab.
Click a cloud session row.
In the list, click Continue here and confirm the review dialog.
Check the chat in this window now shows the session's conversation, and that the handoff is explicit.
items.needs: a cloud session on the same account

items.where: Command palette > Code: Remote Control > Pair a phone; then on the phone, Pair with Desktop
steps: Sign in to AGI in VS Code and open a folder, trusting the workspace.
Run Code: Remote Control from the Command Palette and click Pair a phone.
On the phone, open the Mobile app, choose Pair with Desktop and scan the code.
On the phone, open a local session from this folder and send a message, then check it runs on this computer.
items.needs: a phone with the Mobile app signed in to the same account, a folder open in VS Code, a trusted workspace
items.note: The phone-side wording is taken from the text in the desktop code; the phone app is outside this folder and was not checked.

items.where: Sessions icon in the sidebar header > Cloud tab > Continue in the cloud icon in the sheet header
steps: Click the Sessions icon in the sidebar header and click the Cloud tab.
Click the Continue in the cloud icon (tooltip Continue in the cloud) in the sheet header.
Type a goal, read the review dialog, and click Continue in the cloud to start, or Cancel to stop.
Check the cloud session appears on the Cloud tab with the goal as its title.
items.needs: a folder with a GitHub git remote and a pushed branch, and a signed-in AGI account
items.note: Code line says unfinished: session creation needs AGI_E2B_EXECUTION on in production, so the cloud run may not start.

items.where: Sessions icon in the sidebar header > Cloud tab > click a session row > Bring the branch in
steps: Click the Sessions icon in the sidebar header and click the Cloud tab.
Click a cloud session that has a working branch.
Click Bring the branch in in the list.
If the folder has uncommitted files, read the list of files at stake and decide; then check the branch from the cloud session is checked out locally.
items.needs: a cloud session with a working branch on a GitHub repository, and a local folder with that repository open

items.where: Command palette > Code: Continue in the Cloud > type a goal > review dialog lines What moves and What stays here
steps: Open a folder with a GitHub remote and a pushed branch, with some uncommitted changes if you want to see that line.
Run Code: Continue in the Cloud and type a goal.
Read the review dialog: Repository, Branch, Model, Network, What moves and What stays here.
Click Cancel and check that nothing was started.
items.needs: a folder with a GitHub git remote and a pushed branch

labels.text: What moves: the task you typed and the pushed branch.
What stays here: this chat’s conversation, local tools and servers, and anything not pushed.

items.note: The review dialog is the place the file and environment list is shown; no list of individual files is shown for a cloud move, only the uncommitted count.

items.where: Command palette > Code: Remote Control > Pair a phone
steps: Sign in to AGI in VS Code.
Run Code: Remote Control from the Command Palette and click Pair a phone.
Read the Pairing code and the QR code shown on the panel.
On the phone, scan the code with Pair with Desktop, then check the panel shows Connected to, followed by the phone name.
items.needs: a phone with the Mobile app signed in to the same account

items.where: Command palette > Code: Remote Control > Disconnect phone (while connected); or Command Palette > Code: Stop Remote Control
steps: With a phone connected, run Code: Remote Control from the Command Palette.
Click Disconnect phone and read the Disconnect dialog.
Click Disconnect phone in the dialog.
On the phone, try to follow or steer a session and check it no longer connects.
items.needs: a phone that is paired and connected
items.note: The revoke-from-phone side is not in this folder; the desktop control is shown here.

items.where: No control of its own. Its visible effect is the Remote Control panel status changing to reconnecting and then back to connected
steps: Pair and connect a phone with a session open.
Turn Wi-Fi off on the Mac for a few seconds, then back on.
Run Code: Remote Control and read the status: Connection lost, then Connected to the phone, and check the session on the phone shows the same history.
items.needs: a paired and connected phone, and a way to drop the network connection
items.note: The reconnect step is in the remote control service; resuming the same chat state is in ChatStateManager, which has no separate screen.

items.where: VS Code notification (shown when the VS Code window is not focused): Approval needed, with an Open chat button
steps: Click another app so VS Code is not the focused window.
Start or wait for an approval in a session that is active in this window.
Watch for the notification Approval needed with the Open chat button.
Click Open chat and check the session shows the item waiting for approval.
items.needs: VS Code in the background and a session that can ask for approval
items.note: Notices are posted only while the window is unfocused, and the cross-client source was not verified; the Code line cited sidebarProvider.ts and chatEditorPanel.ts lines that moved.

items.where: Activity Bar > AGI Code icon, then the box "Describe a task…"
steps: Click the AGI Code icon in the Activity Bar (left edge of VS Code).
Click the box that says "Describe a task…", type a short question and press Enter or click Send.
Look for the reply appearing word by word under your message (it streams), and for the turn staying in the chat.
items.needs: a signed-in AGI account or an API key (the code does not state this as a prerequisite; not verified)
items.note: The plan calls it the AGI Workforce view; the code names the sidebar view "AGI Code".

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Open Chat in Editor (also the editor title bar on a file tab)
steps: Open any code file.
Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Open Chat in Editor", press Enter.
Look for a new editor tab named "AGI Chat" next to the code, with the chat inside it and able to send a turn.
Optional: in VS Code's Chat view type @agi and send a question; the reply should come from AGI Code.
items.needs: none

items.where: AGI Code header > Sessions (clock icon) > Local tab; or Command Palette > Code: Show Sessions History
steps: Click the clock icon with the tooltip "Sessions" in the AGI Code header.
Check the "Local" tab lists earlier sessions; the "Cloud" tab lists cloud ones.
Click one session row to reopen it.
Compare: the chosen earlier session should open with its messages.
items.needs: at least one earlier local session and, for cloud, a signed-in account
items.note: The Palette route opens a quick pick titled "Sessions history"; the cloud list depends on sign-in (not verified).

items.where: Sessions history rows show the folder path in their detail line
steps: Open two folders in one VS Code window, start a session in each.
Run Code: Show Sessions History from the Command Palette.
Check that sessions from both open folders are listed and that each row's detail line shows its folder path after the model name.
items.needs: two local folders open in one window, with a session in each
items.note: The code lists threads from every open workspace folder (conversationTreeProvider), so the check is that each row names its own folder.

items.where: Chat composer "Describe a task…": a file-name chip appears by itself when a file is open
steps: Open a code file in the editor and leave it active.
Click into the box "Describe a task…" in the AGI Code sidebar.
Look for a chip with the file's name above the box, and click its × to remove it.
Ask "What file do you see?" and compare the answer with the file that is open.
items.needs: none

labels.text: Attach the active editor file, the current selection and that file's problems to each chat turn.

items.where: Editor right-click > Code: Explain Selection (and Code: Send Selection to a New Chat)
steps: Select a few lines of code in an open file.
Right-click the selection and choose "Code: Explain Selection" (shortcut Cmd+Shift+Alt+E).
Look in the chat composer for a chip named "<file name> selection" and for an explanation of the selected lines.
Compare: the explanation should refer to the selected code only.
items.needs: none

labels.text: Code: Send Selection to a New Chat

items.where: Chat context for an edited but unsaved file
steps: Open a file, type a new function near the top, and do not save it (no Cmd+S).
In the AGI Code box ask "What is the first function in this file?".
Compare the answer with the unsaved text; the saved file on disk does not contain it.
items.needs: a code file you can edit
items.note: Attaching a dirty or untitled buffer is automatic; the setting to save before send defaults to off, so the unsaved text is what is sent.

items.where: Chat composer: type @ followed by a file name; the list is titled "Workspace files and symbols"
steps: Click the box "Describe a task…" and type @ then the first letters of a file name.
Use the arrow keys to pick the file in the list and press Enter.
Type a question about the file and send.
Compare: the answer should use the content of the chosen file.
items.needs: a workspace with files

items.where: Chat composer: type @ then a function or class name; list items read "<name> · <kind> · <path>"
steps: In "Describe a task…" type @ and the name of a function or class from the project.
Look for an item in the same list with a kind word such as function or class and a file path with line numbers.
Pick it with Enter and send a question.
Compare: the attached part should be only the lines of that symbol, not the whole file.
items.needs: a workspace whose language has a VS Code symbol provider (for example TypeScript); without one only files appear (per the code comment)
items.note: The item label format comes from apps/extension-vscode/src/data/mentionSearch.ts (name · kind · path).

items.where: Chat composer chip "{count} problems" (appears by itself); editor right-click > Code: Explain Error
steps: Open a file that has a red error or yellow warning.
Look above the chat box for a chip such as "1 problem" or "N problems".
Right-click the line with the error in the editor and choose "Code: Explain Error" (shortcut Cmd+Shift+Alt+X).
Compare: the reply should explain that error.
items.needs: a file with at least one error or warning
items.note: To fix rather than explain, select the code and use Code: Fix Issue (needs a selection).

items.where: VS Code Settings (Cmd+,) > search "ghost-text inline completions" > turn on AGI Code inline completions (off by default); then type in any code file
steps: Press Cmd+, and search "ghost-text inline completions".
Tick the setting for AGI Code inline completions (it is off by default, user settings only).
Sign in with Code: Sign In to AGI Cloud (or set a key with Code: Set API Key), open a code file, type a few lines and pause.
Look for grey ghost text after the cursor, then press Tab to accept it.
items.needs: the setting turned on in your user settings, a signed-in account or AGI API key, and a trusted workspace

labels.text: Send surrounding code to AGI Cloud for ghost-text inline completions.
Code: Sign In to AGI Cloud

items.note: Inline completions are off in untrusted workspaces (package.json capabilities). Tab acceptance is the standard VS Code inline-suggestion key; the extension does not define its own accept key.

items.where: Select code > right-click > Code: Fix Issue or Code: Refactor Code; then the notice button "Apply Inline"
steps: Select a function in an open file in a trusted workspace.
Right-click the selection and choose "Code: Refactor Code", wait for the reply.
When the notice appears, click "Apply Inline" (or "View in New Tab").
Compare: the selected code in the editor should be replaced in place by the new version.
items.needs: a trusted workspace and a signed-in account or key
items.note: Fix can apply automatically when the autoApplyFixes setting is on; the code shows an in-place edit only when the reply contains a code block.

items.where: Chat approval card > "Review change" (opens VS Code's diff editor); after a turn, "Review changes"
steps: Ask the agent to edit a file in the chat (Ask or Auto mode) and wait for the approval card.
Click "Review change" on the card.
Look for VS Code's side-by-side diff editor showing the original and the proposed file.
Compare the diff with the change described in chat; then use Accept or Reject from the editor.
items.needs: a file the agent can edit, in a trusted workspace

items.where: Chat approval card > "Review change", then revert parts in VS Code's diff editor and approve
steps: Click "Review change" on an approval card that proposes several edits.
In the diff editor, use the revert control on one block to undo only that part (VS Code's own diff control).
Approve the change in chat.
Compare: the file should keep the edits you did not revert.
items.needs: an edit that has more than one separate block

labels.text: Edit it or revert parts, then approve to write your version.

items.note: No separate per-hunk accept button was found in the extension; per-part choice uses VS Code's diff editor and the card's own tooltip text.

items.where: Chat code block > "Apply" button (shows on hover); then the editor's "Accept" link above the change
steps: Ask for a code change so the reply contains a code block, and hover over the block.
Click "Apply" (the button is labelled Opening… while it works).
Look in the open file for the highlighted change with an "Accept" link above it, and click "Accept".
Compare: the file should now contain the suggested code.
items.needs: an open file in the editor (without one the chat shows a warning to open a file)

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Run Terminal Command; terminal right-click > Code: Add Terminal Output to Chat; Code: Continue This Session in the Terminal
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Code: Run Terminal Command", press Enter, type "git status" and press Enter.
Look for a terminal named "Code" that runs the command.
Right-click in the terminal and choose "Code: Add Terminal Output to Chat"; check the output appears as a chip in the chat box.
Optional: run "Code: Explain Terminal Output" from the Command Palette and read the reply.
items.needs: a shell terminal (shell integration helps capture output)

labels.text: Code: Add Terminal Output to Chat

items.note: The terminal is named from PRODUCT_NAMES.code, which reads "Code"; the session-in-terminal command uses a separate terminal named "AGI".

items.where: Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) > type "Code:"
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+P.
Type "Code:" and scroll the list of actions.
Pick "Code: Open Chat" and press Enter.
Compare: the AGI Code chat should open.
items.needs: none

items.where: Keyboard shortcuts: Cmd+K Cmd+S and search "Code:"; defaults include Cmd+Shift+A (Code: Open Chat) and Cmd+Shift+Alt+E (Code: Explain Selection)
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+A anywhere in the editor and check the AGI Code chat opens.
Select some code and press Cmd+Shift+Alt+E.
Press Cmd+Shift+Alt+N and check a new conversation starts.
Compare each result with the action named in the Keyboard Shortcuts list.
items.needs: none (Explain needs a selection)
items.note: Cmd+Shift+A is shared with Code: Accept Current Diff when the cursor is on a proposed diff.

items.where: Status bar, bottom right: the AGI item showing the model and mode; click it to open the model picker (Code: Select Model)
steps: Look at the bottom-right status bar for the AGI item with a model name and a mode word.
Hover it and check the tooltip "click to change model".
Click it, pick a different model in the list.
Compare: the status bar text should show the new model name.
items.needs: none
items.note: The exact status text depends on the active model; the code builds it as an AGI label with the model and mode.

items.where: Chat composer: "Mode and reasoning effort" button (mode icon, left of the model name) and the model pill "Auto"; palette: Code: Choose Agent Mode, Code: Set Reasoning Effort, Code: Select Model
steps: Click the "Mode and reasoning effort" button at the bottom of the composer.
Under "Mode" pick "Plan" (or Ask, Auto, Bypass permissions) and check the button icon changes.
Under "Reasoning effort" pick a level, if the model offers it.
Click the model pill "Auto" and pick another model; check the status bar shows it.
items.needs: a plan that allows the model choice; the effort list appears only for models that take it
items.note: On a plan that uses Auto the code shows an upgrade message instead of a model list.

items.where: Switch to another app while a task runs; a system notice appears with "Allow once", "Deny" and "Open chat"; the Activity Bar icon also shows a badge
steps: Ask the agent for a task that needs a command approval; then click another app so VS Code is not focused.
Wait for the notice "Code: Approval needed." to appear.
Click "Allow once" or "Deny" on the notice.
Compare: the chat should show the decision, and a finished task shows "Task finished" with "Open chat".
items.needs: a task that needs approval, and the VS Code window not focused
items.note: The notices appear only when the VS Code window is not focused (sessionActivityAlert.ts).

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Show Instructions; or Code: Open Settings > "Instructions & editor"
steps: Put an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file in the folder with a short rule, and open that folder.
Open Code: Open Settings and click "Instructions & editor"; look for the file name in the sources list.
Run Code: Show Instructions from the Command Palette and check the same file is offered.
Ask the chat a question that the rule should affect and compare the reply.
items.needs: a folder you can edit with AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or .agiworkforce/instructions.md

items.where: More actions (…) in the AGI Code header > MCP servers / Skills / Plugins / Hooks; or Command Palette > Code: Show MCP Servers, Code: Show Skills, Code: Show Plugins, Code: Show Hooks
steps: Click the "More" (…) button in the AGI Code header.
Choose "MCP servers" and read the list (the quick pick is titled "Code, MCP servers").
Go back and choose "Skills" or "Plugins"; view the list only.
Compare: the list should match what the AGI CLI has configured.
items.needs: none to view; adding a server, skill or plugin runs code, so only view it in testing

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Continue CLI Session Here (CLI session into VS Code); Command Palette > Code: Continue This Session in the Terminal (chat session into a terminal)
steps: In a terminal run the AGI CLI (agi) and send one message so a session exists.
In VS Code press Cmd+Shift+P and run "Code: Continue CLI Session Here"; choose that session.
Check the session opens in the AGI Code chat with its earlier messages.
Back in a chat with a sent message, run "Code: Continue This Session in the Terminal" and check a terminal opens that resumes it.
items.needs: the AGI CLI installed (Code: Install AGI CLI) and a session already started

labels.text: Code: Continue This Session in the Terminal

items.note: The terminal command needs a message sent first; the code shows a notice otherwise.

items.where: Remote-SSH window: Command Palette > Code: Check the CLI in This Environment shows the environment name, e.g. "the SSH host"
steps: Connect the VS Code window to an SSH host with Remote-SSH (VS Code's own command, not in this repo).
Open a folder on that host and press Cmd+Shift+P, run "Code: Check the CLI in This Environment".
Read the message: it should say the CLI runs from a path "in the SSH host".
Open AGI Code and send a message to check replies come from the host.
items.needs: an SSH host you can reach with Remote-SSH, with the AGI CLI installed there

labels.text: Code: Check the CLI in This Environment

items.note: extensionKind is workspace, so the extension runs on the remote host; the Remote-SSH connect step is VS Code's own and not verified here.

items.where: In a dev container window, Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) > Code: Check the CLI in This Environment. WSL is Windows only, so on a Mac only the dev container case applies.
steps: Open the project in a dev container with VS Code's own Remote menu (bottom-left corner, Reopen in Container). This is not an AGI control.
Press Cmd+Shift+P.
Type Check the CLI in This Environment and choose Code: Check the CLI in This Environment.
Read the message. It should name the place it runs (the dev container) and the CLI path there. Compare with Expected: the extension works in the container, not only on the Mac.
items.needs: a dev container set up on this Mac (Docker or a container host) and the AGI CLI installed inside it

labels.text: Code: Check the CLI in This Environment

items.note: The message text is built from a template in src/platform/remoteEnvironment.ts (cliProbeMessage), so the exact wording may differ slightly. Container support is shown through this command and the environment label, not through a separate screen.

items.where: Open a folder in VS Code and choose Don't Trust in VS Code's Restricted Mode prompt (VS Code's own dialog). Then AGI Code sidebar view > Review this workspace first. > Manage trust.
steps: Open a folder in VS Code and choose Don't Trust when VS Code asks about trust.
Click the AGI Code icon in the Activity Bar to open the sidebar view.
Look for the heading Review this workspace first. and the text saying AGI keeps project files and tools disabled while VS Code is in Restricted Mode.
Click Manage trust and check that VS Code's workspace trust page opens. Compare with Expected: the extension explains why it is limited and links to Manage Trust.
items.needs: a folder opened as untrusted (Restricted Mode)
items.note: The Manage trust button runs VS Code's own command (workbench.trust.manage). The card shows only when the onboarding state reports an untrusted workspace; the tester may need to get past the intro first.

items.where: AGI Code sidebar view > Developer runtime needs setup (runtime status panel) > Open setup / Try again. The loading text is Checking the workspace developer runtime…
steps: Click the AGI Code icon in the Activity Bar.
Look for the status panel titled Developer runtime needs setup. Right after opening, it should show Checking the workspace developer runtime… while the check runs.
Click Try again and watch the button change while the check runs.
Click Open setup and check that a setup path opens. Compare with Expected: loading, setup-needed and error states, each with a retry.
items.needs: no AGI CLI available for the folder, to reach the setup state; a network drop or sign-in failure is needed for an error state
items.note: The chat error Retry label comes from a translation key (L10N.retry) whose text was not found in the app folder, so the exact word for that error state is unconfirmed. Whether a network error or sign-in failure produces the error state was not traced.

items.where: VS Code Extensions view > AGI Code > Update (VS Code's own control), then reload the window. The notice reads as product name was updated to version, with a button What’s new. A required update appears as a chat error in AGI Code sidebar.
steps: Install an earlier AGI Code version first, then install the newer version from the VS Code Extensions view and reload the window.
Look for the notice that says the product was updated to the new version, with a button What’s new.
Click What’s new and check that release notes open in the browser.

For the required-update case, the sidebar chat shows Update the extension to continue. Compare with Expected: the user is told an update is needed or available, what changed, and can update. The update button itself is VS Code's, not an AGI control.
items.needs: an earlier AGI Code version installed before the newer one, and a browser for What’s new; the required-update case needs the server to reject the current client version
items.note: The button label for the chat error is a translation key (chatError.updateExtension) whose text was not found in the app folder. The update step itself is VS Code's, not AGI's. The notice only appears when the stored version differs from the new one.

items.where: Shown once on startup in a VS Code build that has no native Chat view. The notice reads AGI Code: [app name] [version] has no native Chat view, so @agi is not available here. Chat runs in the AGI Code sidebar instead. Button: Open chat.
steps: Start VS Code on a build or fork that has no native Chat view (for example an older or modified build).
Look for the notice that says the build has no native Chat view, so @agi is not available here.
Click Open chat and check that the AGI Code sidebar opens.
Start VS Code again and confirm the notice does not repeat. Compare with Expected: the user is told which part is incompatible and where chat runs instead.
items.needs: a VS Code build or fork without the native Chat view; the notice shows only once per install
items.note: The notice depends on the host build lacking the native Chat API; on a normal VS Code build it does not appear. The engines minimum in package.json (vscode ^1.100.0) is enforced by VS Code at install, which is not an AGI message.

items.needs: none

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Select Model > pick a model that cannot read images while the current model can
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+P, type Code: Select Model, press Enter.
Click a model that cannot read images (the app does not label which models read images).
Look for the modal "Switch to ...?" whose detail says it "cannot read images you attach"; compare with Expected.
items.needs: a model that reads images and one that does not (the app does not label this)
items.note: The warning fires on any switch from an image-capable model to a non-capable one, not only when an image is attached. No refusal or reroute of image turns was found in the extension code; the picker does not show image support.

items.where: Command Palette > Code: Select Model > pick a model without tools while the current model has tools
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+P, type Code: Select Model, press Enter.
Click a model that cannot use tools (the picker does not show tool support).
Look for the modal "Switch to ...?" whose detail says it "cannot use tools, so it cannot read or edit files or run commands"; compare with Expected.
items.needs: a model with tools and one without (the app does not label this)

labels.text: cannot use tools, so it cannot read or edit files or run commands

items.note: The only visible tool-capability signal is this switch warning; no refusal of tool-dependent turns was found in the extension code.

items.where: No control of its own; the tool loop and harness catalog hold it
items.needs: none

items.where: No control of its own; a multi-step tool task is only visible as the steps it runs
